title: Partnership allows Highlands to house LCC students
body: Connor Hall, a residence hall on the New Mexico Highlands University campus, on Tuesday. Luna Community College recently signed a Memorandum of Agreement with NMHU to allow Luna students to live at the university in the fall. The students will likely live at Connor Hall. Luna Community College has ensured that at least 65 of its students can live on the New Mexico Highlands University campus in the fall semester following a Memorandum of Agreement signed by leadership at both institutions. The MOA was signed by NMHU Interim President Kimberly J. Blea and LCC President Dr. Carol Linder in late June. The fall semester begins at both institutions on Aug. 17. Blea said in an email statement to The Optic on Tuesday that the collaboration between the institutions demonstrates an “effective stewardship of public resources for the benefit of our students.” “Through this partnership with LCC, we are able to strengthen our community’s support network for students pursuing higher education in Las Vegas,” Blea said. “NMHU has the facilities and LCC has the need for housing.” The agreement comes just one year after Highlands revoked 38 housing contracts it made with Luna students two weeks prior to moving day. NMHU officials said then that those contracts were revoked due to a campus housing shortage that made it challenging for NMHU to house its own students. NMHU officials told The Optic last year that the housing shortage was caused by an increase in student enrollment at the Highlands as well as a partial shutdown of one of its residence halls due to plumbing issues. Linder said Tuesday that it was the students who had an agreement with Highlands for housing last year. The MOA signed by Linder and Blea this summer is a contract between the institutions, not between Highlands and Luna students, Linder said. “It was the students that had contracted with Highlands,” Linder said. “We had an overall understanding that Luna students could have (housing).” The lack of an official MOA put the Luna students in need of housing at a disadvantage, Linder said. The accord was also not the best for Highlands. Because the housing agreement was between Luna students and Highlands, it was up to Luna students to pay Highlands for housing directly. With the MOA in place, Luna students will pay Luna for housing at Highlands. Luna will in turn pay NMHU, Linder said. “We will be putting the housing on our students’ accounts and Luna will be paying Highlands for that housing,” she said. The MOA does not specify which residence hall the Luna students will live in, but Blea said that LCC students will be housed in Connor Hall C-Wing this upcoming academic year. A renovation to this area of the residence hall was recently completed, Blea said. Luna students will pay the same housing rate as NMHU students, Linder said. She said living at Connor Hall costs $2,491 per semester for a double room. All students living in the residence halls must purchase a meal plan, including Luna students. The least expensive meal plan is $2,125 per semester, Linder said, while the most expensive one is about $2,500 per semester. Linder estimated that about 55-65 LCC students will need on campus housing. She said that Luna has reserved 65 beds at Highlands; however, if there are more Luna students in need of housing and there is availability Highlands will accommodate them. Linder said that construction of student housing on the LCC campus is being discussed. She said Luna received $2.8 million in emergency funds from the State Board of Finance last December for housing. Although funding was made available, housing plans have not been approved, she said, but have not been given up on. “We haven’t shut the door on that,” Linder said. “It’s definitely something that is in our longer term plan to have (housing).”     Log In Thank you for taking part in our commenting section. title: New Mexico Highlands University faces another whistleblower retaliation lawsuit
body: The stack of lawsuits filed against New Mexico Highlands University keeps getting taller. Paul Grindstaff, Highlands’ former vice president for advancement and university relations who also served as executive director of the NMHU Foundation, has accused the state-owned school in Las Vegas, N.M., of retaliating against him after he alerted university officials about unsafe athletic facilities and equipment. In a complaint filed Monday in U.S. District Court, Grindstaff alleges Highlands’ regents fired him for whistleblowing and made false accusations against him in a letter sent May 27 to the New Mexico Office of the State Auditor. In addition to containing inaccuracies, his complaint states, the letter “embedded [Grindstaff] in a sweeping narrative of fraud, misconduct, and criminal conduct.” Grindstaff seeks double back pay with interest, reinstatement, compensation for harm to his reputation, attorney’s fees, litigation expenses and other damages. “The Whistleblower Protection Act exists for exactly this case,” Tim White, an attorney representing Grindstaff, said in a statement. “Dr. Grindstaff raised documented safety hazards that were injuring student-athletes at a public university. Weeks later he was fired without a stated reason, and then he was accused of a crime that his accusers’ own records disprove.” Highlands General Counsel Doajo Hicks disputed several of the allegations in the lawsuit, particularly Grindstaff’s claims that the university retaliated against him by submitting a letter to the state auditor or for raising safety concerns. “The University will not try this matter through the media,” Hicks wrote in an email to The New Mexican. “Because the lawsuit concerns personnel matters, disputed facts, and communications with oversight and law enforcement authorities, the University will not comment on specific evidence, individual employees, or the details of any pending review.” Grindstaff’s lawsuit is the latest in a series of scandals to roil Highlands in recent months. The board of regents in May abruptly fired several high-ranking administrators, including Grindstaff, and placed former President Neil Woolf on paid administrative leave, before officially firing him a month later. Woolf has since filed his own lawsuit against the school, alleging retaliation over a construction deal. The regents have denied those accusations, though they did admit to ousting him without cause and said they would comply with the terms of his contract, including “separation pay.” Highlands also faces a harassment and discrimination suit brought by a former athletic director, plus formal probes from the Office of the State Auditor, the state Higher Education Department, and prosecutors from the 4th Judicial District Attorney’s Office and the New Mexico Department of Justice. Grindstaff’s accusations, then, fit somewhere within that web of alleged wrongdoing, lawsuits and government inquiries. He says in his complaint he made a series of “protected disclosures” to university leaders about conditions dangerous to Highlands’ student athletes, including unsafe football helmets and track and turf surfaces that had caused three broken ankles, at least one ACL injury and lower-body injuries to 28 of the 30 women’s soccer players. Woolf and Grindstaff in late 2025 proposed a doomed $85.5 million athletic facilities upgrade that, had it been approved, would have resulted in a new track and field. Rather than responding to his safety concerns, Grindstaff asserts in the complaint, university leaders fired him and named him in the board’s damning letter to the state auditor. The 32-page letter accused Woolf of improper hiring and procurement practices, financial mismanagement and retaliation against university employees, among other misconduct — claims Woolf’s attorney has disputed. But the letter also implicated Grindstaff, alleging he falsified government documents and benefited from preferential hiring practices for members of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, even though he is a lifelong Methodist. The New Mexican obtained the regents’ letter to the state auditor through a public records request and reported on its contents, a disclosure the complaint argues was “foreseeable” and harmful to Grindstaff’s reputation. “A letter to a state oversight agency accusing a named former officer of crimes is a public record subject to inspection, and Defendants knew it,” the complaint states. Grindstaff’s complaint describes the letter as “an attack document rather than a compliance submission” that “accuses a lifelong alumnus, former football student-athlete, major donor, and former volunteer officer of the very Foundation at issue of defrauding the institution he has spent decades supporting.” Hicks, in his email to The New Mexican, wrote the university “supports good faith reporting of safety, compliance, and financial concerns” and “does not retaliate against employees for making protected reports.” The university submitted the letter to the state auditor “in response to an official inquiry” and as part of Highlands’ “continuing cooperation with authorized oversight agencies,” he added. “Personnel decisions are based on legitimate institutional considerations and are reviewed in accordance with applicable law and University policy,” Hicks wrote. Searchlight New Mexico is a nonprofit, nonpartisan media organization that seeks to empower New Mexicans to demand honest and effective public policy. title: Rapist takes plea deal, gets 12 years in prison
body: Editor A Ribera man will spend the next 12 years in prison after pleading guilty to raping a pair of underage girls in July 2025. Joe Louis Rivera, 25, took a plea deal on July 14, pleading guilty to two counts of second degree criminal sexual penetration of a minor. The sentences carry 15-year prison sentences each, along with a four-year enhancement added for being a habitual offender. However, as part of the plea deal with prosecutors, 22 years of the total sentence are suspended and nearly a full year is credited to Rivera for pre-sentencing detention, leaving him with just under 12 years to serve in prison. Also as part of the plea deal, six additional felonies and four misdemeanor charges were dismissed by prosecutors, including two additional counts of criminal sexual penetration of a child, two counts of criminal sexual contact with a child and two counts of contributing to the delinquency of a minor. Upon being released from prison at the end of his sentence, Rivera will be subject to probation for five years to life. The convictions stem from an incident that began on July 25, 2025. According to previous Optic reporting,  deputies with the San Miguel County Sheriff’s Office responded to a home in Ribera after receiving a report that two missing juvenile girls from Las Vegas were at the house. While knocking on a door to the residence, deputies spotted Rivera driving away in a white truck, according to an affidavit filed in San Miguel Magistrate Court. A deputy followed the vehicle onto NM-3 and pulled Rivera over as he turned onto County Road B40B. A deputy found Rivera driving the truck and a teen girl lying down on the passenger seat, the affidavit stated. That girl was one of the underage girls reported missing from Las Vegas. The girl told investigators that at some point during the evening of July 25, she was with Rivera, along with the other girl who’d been reported missing, inside Rivera’s truck. She said Rivera kissed her and forced her to touch him in a sexual manner before he started kissing the other girl, and that he later had intercourse with the other girl. She said the three later went to a house and that while there, Rivera again had intercourse with the other girl and forced her to watch, and forced her to touch him and the other girl, the affidavit stated. Police later located and interviewed the second missing girl. She admitted she’d been drinking with Rivera and said that Rivera had offered her cocaine, the affidavit stated. She told police that early in the night, Rivera was acting “really flirty” toward her, and that he later touched her in a sexual way through her clothing, then began kissing her feet and neck. She said that at one point in the evening, all three of them had gone to Storrie Lake and that Rivera had suggested they both take their pants off and that he forcefully laid his body on top of her. After leaving the lake, the three of them ended up at a house where the girl said she “blacked out,” the affidavit stated. She told police she awoke to Rivera raping her and that the other girl was naked in the bed with them. Rivera was held in jail following his arrest, and will now spend more than a decade behind bars. title: New Mexico Bear stranded atop NM utility pole meets grisly end
body: A bear that climbed to the top of a utility pole in New Mexico reportedly met a grim end after video of the stranded animal began circulating online. The video, which spread across social media, shows a large bear perched high above the ground on a utility pole while a caller contacted emergency dispatchers for help. The person on the phone could be heard telling the 911 operator they were “calling about the bear.” “I’m on Highway 56,” the caller said. The dispatcher appeared to already know about the situation. “Are you calling about a bear?” the operator asked. “It’s on the tower pole?” “Yeah, it’s alive,” the caller responded. But according to the call, wildlife officials had already been contacted, and there were limited options for safely removing the animal. “Just leave it be, I’ve already called Game and Fish, and they said there’s nothing that they can do,” the operator said. “They could go and shoot it and tranquilize it to get it down, but if they do that then it’s gonna fall and hurt itself.” The video shows the bear stuck in a dangerous position at the top of the pole. Later, members of a local New Mexico Facebook group reportedly said the animal died from electrocution, though that account has not been officially confirmed. The incident highlights the strange but real dangers bears can encounter when they wander into human infrastructure. Bears climbing utility poles are not unheard of, especially in rural or semi-rural areas where power lines, poles, and wildlife habitat overlap. 💔 The New Mexico 911 operator: "Are you calling about a bear?" the operator said. "It's on the tower pole?""Yeah, it's alive," the caller responded."Just leave it be, I've already called Game and Fish, and they said there's nothing that they can do. They could go and shoot… In some cases, utility crews have been able to save bears from similar situations by temporarily shutting off power and coaxing them down. In December 2025, a bear in Cochise County, Arizona, was nearly electrocuted after climbing a power pole. A lineman, identified as Werner J. Neubaurer, helped rescue the animal while his wife filmed the encounter. “I de-energized the equipment and worked with a fiberglass stick to get her to climb down,” Neubaurer said, according to USA Today. Video from that Arizona incident reportedly showed Neubaurer using the fiberglass pole to prod the bear until it finally climbed down and ran away safely. The New Mexico situation appears to have ended differently. The dispatcher’s explanation suggested that tranquilizing the bear was considered too risky because the animal could fall from the height and seriously injure itself. Without a safe way to bring the animal down immediately, officials apparently advised leaving it alone while Game and Fish assessed the situation. It remains unclear exactly where along Highway 56 the incident happened, how long the bear had been on the pole, or whether utility workers were called to the scene. It is also unclear whether New Mexico wildlife officials have confirmed the reported electrocution. Still, the video has drawn attention because of the helplessness of the situation: a wild animal alive but stranded high above the ground, with rescue options limited by the very real danger of the fall, the power equipment, and the animal’s own size and behavior. While bear encounters often generate dramatic headlines, the New Mexico video appears to show a different kind of hazard — not an attack, but a tragic collision between wildlife and modern infrastructure. For residents in bear country, officials often urge people to avoid approaching wild animals, keep a safe distance, and contact proper authorities when animals are found in dangerous or unusual locations. In this case, one concerned caller did exactly that. But according to reports from the local Facebook group, the stranded bear’s ordeal may have ended in electrocution before it could be safely removed. title: Law enforcement identifies man suspected of hitting bicyclist south of Durango
body: An Aztec man suspected of hitting a bicyclist Tuesday south of Durango admitted to drinking three beers prior to the crash and had an open bottle of Southern Comfort in the truck, according to an arrest affidavit. Thomas Huntsman, 39, was arrested on suspicion of felony vehicular assault, drunken driving, driving with an open container of alcohol and driving without insurance. He had been released from the La Plata County Jail as of Wednesday. The crash was reported shortly after 6:30 p.m. near County Road 302 and U.S. Highway 550, about 3 miles south of Durango. Bystanders at the scene told authorities the passenger-side mirror hit multiple riders, but only one went down and under the pickup truck and trailer. According to the Colorado State Patrol, Huntsman drifted into a turn lane, hit a cyclist, ran over a stop sign and struck a deer fence. The cycling community identified the injured cyclist as Elliott Saslow, 32, who coaches with Durango Devo, a local cycling group. Saslow suffered broken bones, including a broken pelvis, according to those in the cycling community. He was taken to Mercy Hospital in serious condition. Huntsman refused to participate in a voluntary field sobriety test at the scene of the crash, and a search warrant was granted for an blood-alcohol test, according to the affidavit. While at Mercy Hospital, Huntsman allegedly told law enforcement he was drinking out of a Southern Comfort bottle in the pickup truck. State troopers were unable to locate proof of insurance for Huntsman’s pickup truck. Huntsman was allegedly agitated and aggressive at the scene of the crash. He made statements saying he does not care about cyclists and was vulgar toward cyclists at the scene, according to the affidavit. Todd Wells, a Durango cyclist and former Olympian, arrived at the scene about 10 minutes after the crash. He said Huntsman tried to approach Saslow as he lay on the ground surrounded by other cyclists who were trying to render aid. The driver was acting “belligerent” toward Saslow, Wells said. “The guy who was clearly drunk was trying to get to Elliott and we were trying to keep that person away from Elliott,” he said. Police arrived before any physical altercations could occur between Huntsman and the cyclists, Wells said. Deputies also reported Huntsman standing over the downed cyclist acting aggressive, according to the affidavit. Wells said the typical route for cyclists in that area takes them down Highway 550 for two minutes, as they move from one county road to the next. The turning lane where Saslow was hit is the wider part of the road where drivers have more room to pass. “It’s where you finally feel somewhat safe – where you’re in the shoulder, you’re out of the motorists’ way, there’s plenty of room for passing,” Wells said. title: One killed, two seriously injured in car crash last weekend north of Durango
body: A Durango woman was killed in a three-car crash Saturday on U.S. Highway 550 just north of Durango. Sandra “Sandy” Elliott, 79, was flown to Penrose Hospital in Colorado Springs before succumbing to her injuries, said La Plata County Coroner Jann Smith. The crash was reported about 4:45 a.m. near mile marker 26, according to the Colorado State Patrol. Elliott was traveling north in a Ford Flex when the southbound driver of a Nissan Murano swerved across the center line and hit Elliott head-on, said State Trooper Sherri Mendez. “The front left of the Ford Flex was struck by the front left of Nissan Murano,” she said. The impact sent the Ford Flex rotating and careening off the right side of the road, landing in the northbound ditch. The Nissan then struck the a Toyota Tacoma traveling behind Elliott, pushing it backward from the point of impact. The Nissan then rolled and landed in the southbound lane, Mendez said. The cause of the crash, and whether drugs or alcohol were involved, remained under investigation as of Wednesday. Mendez declined to provide the names of the other parties involved, citing the ongoing investigation. Elliott’s daughter, Allisa Oliger, said Elliott’s partner of five years, Thomas “Steve” Bettis, 76, was a passenger in the vehicle. He suffered critical injuries and was fighting for his life as of Wednesday, she said. Bettis was taken to Penrose in serious condition, she said. The driver of the Nissan, an 18-year-old man, was taken to an unknown hospital with serious injuries. The driver of the Toyota Tacoma, a 26-year-old man, reported no injuries, Mendez said. Elliott is survived by three children and four grandchildren. Her daughter described her as strong-minded, intelligent, brave and truthful. “This was completely unexpected. She was healthy, active, still working with some private clients,” Oliger said. Oliger described her mother as being “at the top of her game.” Elliott, originally from Portland, Oregon, moved to Durango in 1974. She worked as a CPA, starting at Frederick Zink & Elliott, PC, and eventually started her own firm called Elliott Meadows & Associates, LLC. Although she took some private clients, she officially retired around 2015-2017. She was an avid quilter, traveler and golfer. “She lived for golfing,” Oliger said. She was actively involved with Dalton Ranch and previously involved with the League of Women Voters and the Durango Chamber of Commerce. Oliger said both Elliott and Bettis received excellent care from hospital staff as well as from first responders at the scene. jrooney@durangoherald.com  Choose from several print and digital subscription packages Sign up for our daily email newsletter or to receive breaking news delivered to your inbox: © 2026 Tri-City Record |         Ballantine Communications, Inc. title: Republican challenger narrowly outraises N.M. U.S. Rep. Vasquez, but trails with cash on hand
body: New campaign finance reports show that the campaign for an Albuquerque Republican challenging incumbent U.S. Rep. Gabe Vasquez (D-N.M.) in the Nov. 3 general election has narrowly raised more money than his opponent, although Vasquez’s campaign has a strong cash-on-hand advantage. The latest campaign finance filings, which cover April through June, offer a glimpse into a competitive race for a district that represents much of southern New Mexico and a portion of Albuquerque. Vasquez first won election to the 2nd Congressional District seat, which was previously held by Republican Yvette Herrell, in 2022 by less than one percentage point. Greg Cunningham, the Republican nominee who handily won his party’s primary for the race after his opponent bowed out, announced that he raised nearly $902,000 in the second quarter of this year – just shy of $1,000 more than Vasquez. Vasquez’s campaign has about three times the amount of cash on hand, though. “There are some individuals and organizations who feel that CD 2 will be a competitive race. Usually, people don’t like to contribute money unless they feel like the candidate has a shot,” Brian Sanderoff, president of the Albuquerque-based firm Research and Polling Inc., told Source NM. Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham signed off on redrawn congressional districts in late 2021, following the 2020 U.S. Census. That redistricting introduced portions of Albuquerque, which Sanderoff said are considered Democratic strongholds, into the otherwise rural district. “Greg Cunningham does have one challenge to address in whether the mood of the nation could impact his competitiveness … most analysts feel the Democrats will flip the U.S. House,” Sanderoff said. “His strategy is going to have to be to cut his losses in Bernalillo County.” Cunningham in a statement announcing his fundraising efforts said he believes the latest fundraising reports show that district residents want “a Congressman who actually shows up for them, not a far-left radical like Gabe Vasquez who voted to raise taxes on families and against securing our border.” “New Mexico deserves better, and this quarter proves our district is ready to flip,” he wrote. Vasquez’s campaign manager, Patricia Socarras Santiago, in a statement to Source NM, wrote that Cunningham has shown an allegiance to President Donald Trump and raised hundreds of thousands of dollars in “MAGA money.” “New Mexicans cannot be bought off and they deserve someone who is actually fighting for them,” she wrote. “That fighter has always been Gabe Vasquez, and that’s why New Mexicans will re-elect him in November.” Source NM is an independent, nonprofit news organization that shines a light on governments, policies and public officials. title: Abundance of talent on display as Connie Mack World Series begins play this weekend
body: FARMINGTON – The rosters are set and the final planning phases are being made as Friday’s opening day of the pool play portion of the Connie Mack World Series rapidly approaches. Here’s a look at some of the top players coming into the series from across the country that we’ll be keeping an eye on as the series plays out. Browning took part in last year’s CMWS as a member of PPA White Sox Scout Team. A recent commit University of Arkansas, Browning has been one of the top producers for the Pleasant Grove (Texas) Hawks, hitting .363 with seven home runs and 36 runs batted in during his junior season. He was selected to the THSBCA 4A All-State Team as a 1st Team SS and to the TSWA 4A All-State Team as a 3rd Team SS. Sullivan, who pitched for the Redskins in last year’s CMWS, stands at 6-foot, 188 pounds and has a fastball consistently in the mid-90s that has reached as high as 97 miles per hour. As a senior at Walsh Jesuit (Ohio) High, Sullivan went 3-1 with a 0.90 ERA and 89 strikeouts in 46.2 innings. His career ERA was 1.30 ERA over 145 innings with 256 strikeouts. The Warriors finished the season as Division II state runners-up. Sullivan plans to play college ball next season at the University of Tennessee. Another returning starter from last year, Viars has grown on and off the field to become one of the most important players on this summer’s roster. “He has really grown up even beyond what he was last year,” said D-Bat head coach Ryan Bonesio. “He had a hit peak around .400, and he was one of the state leaders in home runs. That's to go with the fact that his impact defensively is unmatched.” Viars, a recent commit to West Virginia, has the potential to be something special as a catcher. “I know that he's got an opportunity to work into eventually becoming a catcher at West Virginia, as well,” Bonesio said. “He's a fantastic player and he's going to be a big part of how we do in this tournament.” The recent Baylor commit comes off an impressive season at Montgomery (Texas) High School, in which he recorded a .387 batting average with six home runs, 25 runs batted in and 17 stolen bases. A star infielder at Boswell High School in Fort Worth, Thacker has also excelled at powerlifting, recently winning the Texas Class 6A state title in the 181-lb. weight class, lifting a career-best total of 1,630 pounds. Thacker has played a dozen games for the D-Bat United this summer, recording a .273 batting average with 10 runs batter in and 11 runs scored. “Thacker is a defender and a good bat,” said Bonesio. “He's a pretty good pitcher too, so we like to use him in the middle to bottom third of the lineup.” Thacker has also been proficient on the mound as a relief pitcher for D-Bat United, striking out seven and allowing just four hits over five innings of work. He is currently committed to playing baseball at Navarro College in Corsicana. An incoming senior at Anderson (Texas) High School and commit to the University of Texas, Rippy has been a member of the team from the beginning of the summer. Rippy is coming off a strong high school season, in which he earned Most Valuable Player honors and Offensive Player of the Year. Blue Valley (Kansas) High’s Ethan Carswell is a switch-hitting middle infielder who recently announced his intent to play collegiate ball at the University of Southern California. Carswell batted .308 for the Redbirds this summer. A recent commit to the University of Texas after having recently graduate from Waxahachie (Texas) High, Robinson finished third among Class 6A baseball players with 11 home runs this past season. He finished the season with 61 runs batted in and only seven strikeouts. title: Fanfare and excitement build as Connie Mack World Series opens Friday at Ricketts Park
body: FARMINGTON – The game can change in the blink of an eye. One minute, your favorite team is up four runs and three outs away from securing a victory. Before you know it, a base hit follows a walk and a hit batter, and suddenly you can feel the drama build. From the perspective of a player or manager, the swings and shifts in momentum can be physically taxing. For the fan — trust me — it’s a whole different experience. As a passionate lover of baseball, I’m also the first to admit that the world is coming to an end when my favorite team loses what might well be a meaningless game in the first week of May. I’m also the guy who will break down why a supposedly meaningless win by that same team the very next day is precisely why it will win the division, the league and, eventually, the World Series. That’s the seesaw lifestyle of baseball fans. The stars have to align a certain way. The decisions made in clubhouses and owners boxes that are completely out of our control are the very reason we pore over box scores and transactions. Supporters of high school, collegiate or travel teams go through many of the same emotional conflicts. Tack on the costs of being a booster or a coach responsible for keeping the team fed and transported from one place to another, and suddenly the passion for the sport becomes deeply personal and quite expensive. These are important things to remember when you’re sitting in the stands and chiding the decisions made by a coach or a manager. Not only is he keeping his eye on the action occurring on the field, but he is also responsible for making sure his team will be ready to play later tonight or tomorrow. Or, as will be the case for a majority of teams this week, he is balancing the plans that have to be made for that uncomfortable trip home. The Connie Mack World Series will be one of a few massive moments in the careers of rising baseball talents. For some, it may be their final moment on the field. For a few others, it may be just the beginning. In addition to the historic names of Ken Griffey, Jr., Barry Larkin and Edgar Martinez, who graced the field at Ricketts Patrk before combining to hit more than 1,100 home runs in their respective careers in Major League Baseball, there’s names you may not be as familiar with who’ve also had a significant impact on their MLB rosters. Yan Gomes was an MLB All-Star catcher and World Series champion with the 2019 Washington Nationals who will be enshrined in the Connie Mack World Series Hall of Fame this week. Gomes competed in the Connie Mack World Series with the Florida Bombers of Miami. Born in Mogi das Cruzes, Gomes went on to build an outstanding Major League career with the Toronto Blue Jays, Cleveland Guardians, Washington, Oakland Athletics, and Chicago Cubs. And if you’re looking for current stars linked to the CMWS, look no further than New York Mets starting right fielder Carson Benge, who was one of the stars for the 2023 Enid (Oklahoma) Majors. Either way, it’s up to you to respect the moment and the sport. If that’s your favorite team rushing out to celebrate the championship, cheer loud and proud. If that’s not your team showering the winning coach with a Gatorade bath following the conclusion of the CMWS, that’s alright, too. We’ve all been on both sides of that celebratory moment, and that’s precisely why we love baseball. Because it’s just a matter of days before we do it all over again. Enjoy the tournament. title: Pair of Farmington High grads sign to extend athletic careers
body: FARMINGTON – A pair of multi-sport athletes recently graduated from Farmington High School recently announced their intention to extend their academic and athletic careers by signing on with colleges. Danny Hagstrom, who doubled as a pitcher and outfielder this past season for the Scorpions, signed his letter of intent to join the baseball roster at Lassen Community College in Susanville, California. Hagstrom, who achieved success both in baseball and football at Farmington High, joins a Cougars baseball team coming off a 28-15 season and advancing to the California Community College Athletic Association postseason. Hagstrom was a solid contributor on the field. Among his season highlights at the plate last season was a 3-RBI performance including a home run in a district clash at Rio Rancho last April, followed by a 4-for-5 game against Cleveland High. The Cougars, coached by Frank Avilla, have been a powerhouse in junior college baseball in recent years. Under Avilla’s leadership, the Cougars recorded their most wins in over 20 years in 2022, 2024 through 2026, and tallied over 120 program wins across the past five seasons. The Cougars have now made five consecutive NORCAL Regional appearances (2022–2026), and in both 2024 and 2025, Lassen had the honor of hosting back-to-back NORCAL Regionals—the first time that’s happened since 2004. Avilla is entering his 17th season with Lassen College baseball and his 16th as head coach. His teams have averaged 20-plus wins per season since 2017. Hagstrom was also a key contributor on the FHS football team, recording nearly 100 tackles in three seasons on the Scorpions football team. Also signing his letter of intent was recent Farmington High graduate Santiago Gonzales, who has agreed to attend Allan Hancock College in Santa Maria, California. Gonzales played a variety of sports during his 4-year stint at FHS, including football, track and field, baseball and wrestling. On the gridiron, Gonzales doubled as a linebacker and running back, recording nearly 200 tackles in three seasons as a Scorpion. The Bulldogs, coming off a 4-6 campaign last season, are a part of the Western State Conference and are led by head coach Rick Aguilar. title: Former New Mexico AG says federal prosecutors haven’t honored Epstein investigation agreement
body: Federal prosecutors investigating the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein “to this day” have not upheld an agreement to share New Mexico-related materials with the state’s top law enforcement agency, former New Mexico Attorney General Hector Balderas wrote in a Monday letter to Attorney General Raúl Torrez. Balderas’ letter says that his office was conducting an investigation into Epstein and his Santa Fe County property, Zorro Ranch, in 2019 when they learned of a broader federal investigation into Epstein and his co-conspirator Ghislaine Maxwell. He wrote that his office and the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of New York subsequently came to an agreement weeks before Epstein’s suicide – Balderas’ investigators would stop interviewing potential witnesses, and the federal prosecutors would refer state-related matters to the New Mexico attorney general’s office at the end of their case. “The agreement with the SDNY prosecutors was not to simply stop or to stay out of their way. Instead, my administration had a firm agreement with the SDNY that they have not honored to this day,” Balderas wrote to Torrez Monday, adding that partially redacted files released under the federal Epstein Files Transparency Act contain handwritten notes confirming the details of the arrangement. Balderas’ letter comes weeks after Torrez accused the federal government of impeding his agency’s investigation into Zorro Ranch. He has contended that the U.S. Department of Justice has delayed the release of relevant records that contain names of witnesses, abuse survivors and co-conspirators that his agency needs if it is to fully investigate and prosecute any criminal matters. “Former Attorney General Balderas has confirmed something we’ve said all along: New Mexico honored its side of an agreement with the federal government, and the federal government did not honor its own,” Torrez said in a statement Tuesday. “That breach doesn’t weaken our position, it strengthens it. New Mexico is entitled to these records, and we will use every tool available, including litigation, to obtain them.” Source NM is an independent, nonprofit news organization that shines a light on governments, policies and public officials. title: Speed Merchant heads field of six in $75,000 Road Runner
body: ALBUQUERQUE -- Trainer Todd Fincher brings Speed Merchant back to the races off a five-month layoff and will face five rivals in the $75,000 Road Runner Stakes, the featured event on Sunday's program at Albuquerque Downs. Owned by Dale F Taylor Racing LLC, Speed Merchant is a perfect 3-for-3 over the Albuquerque Downs course, including a win in the New Mexico State Fair Thoroughbred Futurity. Bred in New Mexico by Brad King and Chris Coleman, the son of Marking has won five of seven career starts and earned more than $335,000. The Road Runner Stakes, a 5 1/2 furlong sprint for state-bred 3-year-olds, will be run as the ninth race with a scheduled post time of 4:50 p.m. A three-time stakes winner, Speed Merchant also scored victories in the Hobbs Fall Classic last November at Zia Park, then opened his 3-year-old campaign with a narrow victory in the Corralito Steak House Stakes. In his most recent start, he was second in the Red Hedeman Mile in his first start around two turns. Speed Merchant will break from post five in the six-horse field and will be ridden by Alfredo Juarez, Jr., coming off a strong season at Lone Star Park where he finished eighth in the thoroughbred standings, winning 24 races from 171 starts. Trainer Dick Cappellucci will send out a pair of starters in the Road Runner, including the unbeaten Driving Money. The son of Conquest Mo Money, owned by Judge Lanier Racing and bred by McKenna Thoroughbreds, is 2-for-2 including a win in the Kendrick Stakes at SunRay Park last May and has earned more than $60,000. Driving Money will break from post three in the Road Runner Stakes and will be ridden by Oscar Andrade, Jr. Cappellucci will also saddle Vanishing Money, a two-time winner from four starts with earnings of nearly $47,00. The son of Conquest Mo Money will break from the outside post under jockey Miguel Perez. title: ESPN starts layoffs tied to NFL Network acquisition, memo says
body: ESPN is undergoing a significant round of layoffs for the first time in three years after taking over NFL Network in April. Chairman Jimmy Pitaro said in a memo to employees Tuesday morning, obtained by The Associated Press, that most moves are the result of ESPN’s acquisition of NFL Network and other league digital assets last year. The deal was announced last August and also included NFL Fantasy and the rights to distribute the RedZone channel to cable and satellite operators. In return, the NFL got a 10% equity stake in ESPN. It was approved by government regulators in January. NFL Network employees became part of ESPN on April 1. “Over the past several months, we’ve made significant progress integrating the NFL assets that we acquired into ESPN,” Pitaro wrote in the memo. “Throughout this process, we have taken the time to carefully evaluate our collective teams, resources and organizational structure to best position us for the future. As a result, we had to make some difficult decisions about job impacts that we will be communicating today. “While most of the job impacts are tied to the acquisition, we will also notify colleagues in other parts of the company today that their positions have been impacted. We are committed to treating employees with compassion and respect and to providing support as they navigate this transition.” While most of the layoffs affect production and behind-the-scenes personnel, some on-air talent were affected. Ryan Clark, who joined ESPN in 2015 as an NFL analyst, learned of his layoff while on “NFL Live” on Monday. A person familiar with the situation said Clark was originally going to be told Tuesday morning before reports leaked about the decision. Clark was told by company executives rather than hear about it elsewhere. He did not finish his appearance on the show. The person spoke to the AP on condition of anonymity because they were not at liberty to discuss personnel decisions. Clark took to social media on Tuesday to address the layoffs. He also shared a video of himself working out. “Sending prayers and love to all those laid off today by ESPN. So many of you have poured your life into that company, & I know how you’re feeling right now,” Clark wrote on X. “My hope is as this door closes another opens for you all. God bless!” Other notable names include Karl Ravech, who had been with ESPN since 1993 and had been an integral part of its baseball coverage. Ravech was the voice of “Sunday Night Baseball” from 2022-25 before the package moved to NBC this season. He did call Monday night’s game between the Los Angeles Dodgers and Philadelphia Phillies. Tom Pelissero, who had been with NFL Network since 2017, is also part of the cuts. ESPN had recently signed NFL insiders Ian Rapoport and Adam Schefter to extensions. The ESPN cutbacks are also part of other reductions that are taking place throughout the Walt Disney Company this week. title: New Mexico lawmakers express frustration with long process to rebuild behavioral health system
body: Democratic and Republican New Mexico lawmakers expressed frustration Monday over the slow rollout of a program meant to revive the state’s behavioral health system. An executive committee overseeing the effort has reviewed plans to rebuild behavioral health infrastructure across the state after Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham in early 2025 signed Senate Bill 3, known as the Behavioral Health Reform and Investment Act, into law. The legislation sought to identify and address gaps in the state’s behavioral health system after Republican Gov. Susana Martinez accused several providers of fraud and froze their Medicaid payments, prompting many to pull their operations out of New Mexico. At the outset, the committee carved New Mexico into 13 behavioral health “regions,” mirroring the state’s 13 judicial districts, and asked local governments in each region to file plans that highlight the unique needs and goals in each of their respective communities. To date, the committee has only approved plans for Region 1 and Region 2, which cover the Santa Fe and Albuquerque areas, although several more are anticipated to face votes at the committee’s August meeting. In the nearly 18 months since Lujan Grisham signed the legislation, local leaders have often expressed confusion as to how they go about drafting their regions’ plans. State Rep. Elizabeth “Liz” Thomson (D-Albuquerque), who chairs the interim Legislative Health and Human Services Committee, at a Monday hearing said she and other lawmakers have had to occasionally correct the record because of that confusion. She cited constituents who have spoken during public comment periods at recent meetings and falsely stated that the state government, rather than local officials, is mandating the specific expenditures laid out in regional plans. “It’s a something-show. I’ll just say that,” Thomson said. Some lawmakers during Monday’s hearing also questioned whether the state should have more involvement. If there are 13 diverse, sprawling regions, shouldn’t there be a statewide plan to keep things on track, they asked? “Y’all have articulated today exactly my skepticism with Senate Bill 3,” Sen. Larry Scott (R-Hobbs) told presenters during Monday’s hearing. “No strategic plan, no agency or individual ultimately responsible for the development of a statewide program.” Nick Boukas, who chairs the executive committee overseeing the regional plans and works as director of the state Health Care Authority’s Behavioral Health Services Division, responded that he and his colleagues do plan to create a statewide strategic plan. They are waiting until all 13 regional plans are in place before they create a statewide plan so they can identify areas of common concern across the state, he said. “It doesn’t make sense, in my opinion, to create a strategic plan when we don’t know what the regions are focusing on,” Boukas said. “If 10 of the 13 regions are identifying crisis and we leave that out, shame on us – we’re not listening to the folks that are creating these plans.” Source NM is an independent, nonprofit news organization that shines a light on governments, policies and public officials. title: Mental illness, substance abuse driving New Mexico’s high maternal mortality, new data shows
body: Mental illness, particularly substance abuse, was the biggest contributing factor to 74 pregnancy-related deaths of New Mexico mothers between 2018 and 2023, according to new data presented Monday to a legislative health committee. New Mexico Department of Health officials presented the most recent figures from the department’s Maternal Mortality Review Committee, a board tasked with investigating all deaths that occur during or within one year of pregnancy and recommending measures to prevent such deaths in the future. According to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, New Mexico’s maternal mortality rate is well above the national average. Still, the new data shows that New Mexico’s pregnancy-related mortality rate has dropped precipitously since the COVID-19 pandemic. In 2021, the state’s pregnancy related-mortality rate – was 149.6 per 100,000 live births. By 2023, however, the rate decreased by nearly 84% to just 24.2, according to the new data. The rate the New Mexico Mortality Review Committee measures is the number of people who die due to pregnancy complications or from health conditions a pregnancy exacerbated. The decline brought levels back to pre-pandemic rates. Nonetheless, the review committee noted that more than 97% of the 74 deaths in that six-year period were “preventable.” The report identifies mental illness as the biggest factor underlying those deaths, a term that includes suicide, substance abuse and post-traumatic stress disorder, among other psychiatric illnesses. Mental illness accounted for nearly 42% of the deaths, followed by infections at roughly 16% and heart-related illnesses and hemorrhages or other injuries that each caused approximately 10% of the deaths. “Mental health conditions, especially substance use disorders, remain the most significant contributing factor to maternal mortality and the most common underlying cause of death,” NMDOH Chief Medical Officer Miranda Durham told lawmakers. The review committee also determined that more than three-quarters of the patients who died in that period had no prenatal care or unknown prenatal care, according to the new data. Kevin Peine, executive director at the NMDOH’s Centers for Public Health, noted that the rate of deaths drops sharply even if patients receive prenatal care only in their first trimester. “This drives home the point to me that access to prenatal care in the state is critical, and early prenatal care can be a driving factor towards some of those preventions,” he said. Several Democratic lawmakers on the interim Health and Human Services Committee keyed in on the findings regarding lack of prenatal care and substance abuse to criticize Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham’s 2025 order requiring state officials to take immediate custody of newborns with fetal alcohol syndrome or drug exposure. Committee Chair Rep. Liz Thomson (D-Albuquerque) said she fears that mothers with drug addictions will opt out of prenatal care to avoid losing custody of their babies. “That’s really scary to me, and something I think that we need to keep a close eye on,” she said. State Sen. Linda Lopez (D-Albuquerque) also said the report shows the state’s resources would be better placed supporting mothers and babies exposed to drugs, rather than separating them. The report recommended expanding post-birth support, conducting additional screenings and expanding services to high-risk families in the period right before and right after birth. “Separating a newborn from a new mom is trauma in itself,” Lopez said. “If we’re willing to separate and take away, then what is the state not doing to assist and help these new moms?” Michael Coleman, Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham’s communications director, did not respond to Source NM’s request for comment Monday, though he recently told Source NM that the governor stands behind the directive. “The governor believes safety is the top priority – and that means giving parents the space they need to recover, while making sure no baby is left in a home where exposure puts them at risk,” he said. title: Opening statements made in Farmington man’s double-homicide trial
body: It’s a case about “deliberate choices,” and according to the prosecution, Andrew Whittenberg made the choice on Oct. 21, 2024, to kill two people. Special Prosecutor Andrea Reeb in the opening statement of Whittenberg’s double-homicide trial said “the defendant made serious and deliberate choices – armed himself by stealing a gun, hunted down a woman he wanted to kill and when another person stood in the way of him wanting to escape, he made another choice and raised a gun killing another person.” Whittenberg, 36, was charged with two counts of first-degree murder, aggravated burglary, a second-degree felony; tampering with evidence, a third-degree felony; possession of a firearm by a felon, a third-degree felony; and larceny of a firearm, a fourth-degree felony. The charges are in connection with the shooting deaths of Kelly Heath, 45, and Brent Francis, 24, both of Farmington. The five-day trial began at 3 p.m. July 20 after the jury was seated. Daniel Gallego, a forensic pathologist for the Office of the Medical Investigator, was the first to testify and detail the deaths. Gallego said Heath was killed by a single gunshot wound to the head. It “entered through the right side of the face, went through the spinal cord” and “was associated with skull fractures and bleeding around the brain.” It exited the back of the head and caused a nearly instant death. Reeb told the jury that Whittenberg was looking for Heath the morning of the killing and was asking for “Kelly” when he reportedly broke into a house on Kayenta Drive and stole an AR-15. Heath was found dead in her driveway at 5:45 a.m. by Farmington Police, and by that time, Whittenberg had “moved to the Ralph Miller business,” Reeb said. An employee of the business will testify that he “heard a banging on the door,” Reeb said. When he opened the door, he found Whittenberg “agitated.” Reeb said, “He wants a ride. He’s holding this AR-15.” The witness “gets him to go outside the business and stand on the porch” where he reportedly fired multiple shots into a pickup truck driven by Francis, who arrived at 5:44 a.m. at work and was “sitting in his truck eating a breakfast burrito,” Reeb said, adding she will show the jury videos of Whittenburg firing into the truck. Francis was shot multiple times. He had at least three gunshot wounds to the head and one to his back, according to Gallego, who said the “lethal trauma is concentrated around the head.” Gallego stated that Francis suffered a “catastrophic injury,” which “was caused by another human being pulling a trigger.” Francis’ mother, Jennifer Tom, testified and said her son “was always outgoing. Everybody got along with him. He was always helping out whoever needed help. He wanted to help out as many people as he could.” Francis did not know Whittenberg, Tom said. No one in their family knew him. Heath’s daughter, Kristianna Heath also testified saying that her mother had a “past relationship” with Whittenberg, but she “never really seen them interact with one another.” Kristianna described her mother as being “Very bubbly, very outgoing, always walking around with a smile on her face. You were guaranteed to leave the room with a smile on your face, if you were around her.” When Reeb showed the jury graphic photos of Heath’s dead body, Whittenberg looked down and away. His defense attorney Marie Legrand Miller patted him on the shoulder. Legrand Miller told the jury that “Andrew Whittenberg is a person who has been wrongfully accused of crimes he did not commit.” She said, “This isn’t a case about a man making choices. This isn’t a case about Andrew Whittenberg committing horrible crimes.” Legrand Miller told the jury that Whittenberg had been “using drugs, wandering around the city,” and this “put him in a situation where his credibility was poor.” She admitted the deaths were “tragic,” but said that there will be “lots of reasonable doubt that Andrew Whittenberg committed these horrible crimes.” Reeb said she will present a timeline, video, forensic experts and eyewitnesses to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that “there was a quality in (Whittenberg’s) thinking of premeditation to all of these crimes.” “Our lives are often defined by deliberate choices we make… . His choices and his decisions in this matter shows you his exact intent,” Reeb said. Since his arrest on Oct. 21, 2024, Whittenberg picked up additional charges while being held in the San Juan County Detention Center. He was charged with two counts of battery on a peace officer for reportedly smashing an officer’s hand in a door. Whittenberg also was charged with possession of a weapon or explosive by a prisoner for allegedly making a weapon from the top of a broken chain link fence in the pod, where he had been housed, according to the affidavit for arrest warrant. He reportedly told another detainee that he was planning to use it “to hurt a detention center guard, and then possibly escape from custody “if his jury trial does not go in his favor,” the affidavit said. dmayeux@tricityrecordnm.com  Choose from several print and digital subscription packages Sign up for our daily email newsletter or to receive breaking news delivered to your inbox: © 2026 Tri-City Record |         Ballantine Communications, Inc. title: HPCC Fire map honored with international GIS award
body: The story of the devastating 2022 Hermit’s Peak/Calf Canyon Fire and its aftermath gained a new international audience and an award during the recent Esri User Conference in San Diego, Calif. Dana Heusinkveld, a GIS research specialist with the New Mexico Forest and Watershed Restoration Institute (NMFWRI) based at Highlands University, designed a beautiful poster with a map and text describing the events leading up to the wildfire that burned more than 340,000 acres in northern New Mexico, burned hundreds of houses and other buildings, and was followed by damaging post-fire floods. Her map was awarded first place in Place Perception, one of a dozen categories at the July 13-17 conference that attracted more than 600 entries from around the globe. In their comments, Esri judges said "this map delivers a powerful sense of progression through its skillful use of color and composition. The growth of the fire unfolds naturally across the page while the chart colors are beautifully coordinated with the map, reinforcing the story and creating a unified design." The Esri Users Conference brings together GIS practitioners from across the country and globe to share ideas, techniques, and inspiration for geospatial applications and storytelling. See Heusinkveld's map and other maps in various categories at https://www.esri.com/en-us/about/events/uc/agenda/map-gallery-awards#place-perspective-award NMFWRI’s GIS team also presented to more than 100 GIS colleagues at the conference regarding the HPCC Post-fire Resource Hub. The team, which includes program manager Patti Dappen, Katie Withnall, Heusinkveld, also presented on a ReSHAPE, a program and online tool to collect and analyze data on fuel treatment projects and wildfires at the national level. ReSHAPE is a joint effort under the Southwest Ecological Restoration Institutes, of which NMFWRI is a member. Find out more at https://reshapewildfire.org/home     Log In Thank you for taking part in our commenting section. title: HHS New Mexico NM woman pleads guilty in $4M Medicaid fraud scheme
body: A Farmington woman has pleaded guilty in federal court after prosecutors say she helped carry out a years-long Medicaid fraud scheme involving fake and ineligible non-emergency medical transportation trips across New Mexico. Dorothea Irving, 47, pleaded guilty Monday to conspiracy to commit health care fraud, according to the U.S. Department of Justice. Prosecutors say Irving worked with a non-emergency medical transportation company to submit millions of dollars in false claims to New Mexico Medicaid for trips that either did not happen or were not eligible for reimbursement. The alleged scheme took place between 2020 and 2026, while Irving worked as a driver for a company that provided non-emergency medical transportation, commonly known as NEMT. New Mexico Medicaid covers transportation for eligible Medicaid recipients who need help getting to non-emergency medical services, such as routine doctor appointments, when they do not have access to a personal vehicle or public transportation. But according to court documents, Irving and others used the program as part of a multi-year fraud scheme. Instead of simply transporting Medicaid beneficiaries to legitimate medical appointments, Irving, the company, its owner, employees, and other drivers submitted false trip records claiming that Irving or her children were Medicaid beneficiaries who needed transportation. Prosecutors say the false records included trips that never happened, claims that Irving acted as an attendant for her children on their own trips, and paperwork in which drivers falsely claimed to have transported one another to appointments. Federal prosecutors said those records were used to disguise the fact that drivers were actually driving themselves. In many cases, the fraudulent trip records involved Irving, other drivers, or minor children supposedly traveling long distances across New Mexico to Alcoholics Anonymous meetings. The DOJ said the NEMT company then used the false trip records to submit millions of dollars in fraudulent claims to New Mexico Medicaid. In some cases, the company allegedly claimed each passenger in a vehicle had taken a separate trip, multiplying the amount billed to taxpayers. For trips involving Irving and her children as the supposed Medicaid recipients without transportation, the company submitted approximately $3,957,788 in fraudulent claims and received approximately $4,142,942 from Medicaid, according to the Justice Department. Irving herself received approximately $980,901 from the company over four years of the scheme. The guilty plea marks another major Medicaid fraud case in New Mexico, where taxpayer-funded programs have repeatedly drawn scrutiny over waste, fraud, and weak oversight. The case also highlights how programs intended to serve vulnerable patients can be exploited when providers and insiders manipulate billing records. Irving faces a maximum penalty of 10 years in prison. A sentencing date has not yet been scheduled. Her sentence will be determined by a federal district court judge after review of the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other legal factors. The case is being investigated by the FBI, the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General, IRS Criminal Investigation, and the New Mexico Medicaid Fraud Control Bureau. The announcement was made by Assistant Attorney General Colin M. McDonald of the Justice Department’s National Fraud Enforcement Division; FBI Albuquerque Special Agent in Charge Justin A. Garris; HHS-OIG Special Agent in Charge Jason E. Meadows; IRS-CI Acting Special Agent in Charge Scott Brown of the Phoenix Field Office; and New Mexico Medicaid Fraud Control Bureau Director Jessica Randall. Trial Attorney Lauren Randell of the Justice Department’s Criminal Division Fraud Section and Assistant U.S. Attorney Katherine Lewis for the District of New Mexico are prosecuting the case. The DOJ noted that the case falls under its broader effort to crack down on fraud against federal benefit programs. In April, the department announced the creation of the National Fraud Enforcement Division, which it described as “laser-focused” on investigating and prosecuting fraud against the American people. That work supports President Donald Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a government-wide effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance targeting fraud, waste, and abuse in federal benefit programs. Since 2007, the DOJ’s Health Care Fraud Strike Force Program has charged more than 6,200 defendants accused of collectively billing federal health care programs and private insurers more than $45 billion. New Mexico acequia advocates renew effort for disaster funding amid floods, fires and drought
body: New Mexico Acequia Association Executive Director Paula Garcia, pictured at the Roundhouse on July 15, 2026, said accessible, recurring funding for acequias is increasingly urgent due to natural disasters that deprive stewards of their livelihoods. New Mexico acequias won’t survive the new normal of wildfires, floods and prolonged drought without a dedicated, easy-to-access funding stream that operates independently of state or federal disaster response systems. That’s the conclusion New Mexico Acequia Association Executive Director Paula Garcia told Source NM she reached following a series of legislative committee hearings this week. The interim Land Grant Committee convened budget experts and advocates to discuss how to craft legislation that would provide the historic irrigation canals with adequate funding to rebuild after increasingly common and damaging natural disasters. In recent years, wildfires, floods and drought have weakened the statewide acequia network, causing tens of millions of dollars in damage each year and depriving irrigators of their livelihoods until they can pay to dig out sediment, replace a headgate or rebuild an embankment, Garcia said. But funding from state and federal disaster response agencies has been difficult to access. Most disaster funding hinges on whether an official state or federal declaration has been declared, but sometimes disaster damage to acequias escapes the notice of state or federal leaders, Garcia said. For example, last year, she noted, floods that damaged roughly 30 acequias near Chimayo and Ojo Caliente did not prompt a state disaster declaration. More recently, stewards of an acequia in the Jemez area are similarly trying to rebuild without state or federal funding following a flood that destroyed it earlier this summer, she said. “In the [current] disaster framework, it’s just not considered important enough to rise to the level of a disaster, but you’ve got dozens of acequias silted in, and millions of dollars of help they need,” Garcia told Source NM. But even if state or federal leaders declare a disaster, the small, volunteer organizations overseeing the ditches often don’t have the capacity to navigate layers of bureaucracy to unlock funding. And in most cases, acequias have to pay 25% of the costs or find a way to pay for repairs in full and then wait for slow-to-arrive government reimbursement. That leaves acequias increasingly vulnerable to disasters, Garcia said, with nowhere to turn. “There is no clarity on what to do, no clear place that serves acequias specifically in the way that they need to be served,” she said. Similar legislation has failed to clear more than one committee in recent years. Last year, House Bill 371 would have established a trust fund that generated $5 million a year for acequias to rebuild after disasters. It passed the House of Representatives by a 63-2 vote but failed to pass the Senate Finance Committee. Garcia said she hopes the ongoing meetings with lawmakers and others in the months leading up to the session will produce legislation that “cracks the code” and finally dedicates adequate funding for acequias struggling for their survival.. “We need to cultivate that political will to make it happen, and make the case about why our communities are important,” she said. “We’re a part of New Mexico, and our infrastructure needs are very unique and vital to our survival as land-based people.” This post first appeared at sourcenm.com     Log In Thank you for taking part in our commenting section. title: Dem Race For Lt. Governor Reveals A Strain Of Socialism Has Now Found A Home In The State's Majority Party; Haaland Falls Behind What Was Her Own Left Wing As Pope And Garcia Richard Seek Support
body: Sen. PopeThe race for lieutenant governor is revealing a much more aggressive left wing in the state Democratic party with important implications for economic policy should Deb Haaland become the next governor. The race for the number two spot features two leading hopefuls--term-limited State Land Commissioner Stephanie Garcia Richard and ABQ state Senator Harold Pope. Their below-the-radar contest is to fill the vacancy created when Secretary of State Maggie Toulouse Oliver won the primary nomination over Pope but withdrew for health reasons. The race will be decided by about 500 members of the party's State Central Committee in a four-day electronic vote July 25-29. The party's more pronounced left wing was in evidence at the June primary election when moderate Democrats failed to muster respectable percentages in even conservative counties such as Eddy, Chaves and Lea, revealing that middle of the road politics is practically extinct among the party's nominating wing.Now the Pope-Garcia Richard battle unveils party progressives even going after Haaland who is being labeled a "corporate Democrat" by some supporters of Pope. That is quite the turn of events given that Haaland was elected to the ABQ congressional seat and in 2018 immediately caucused with the progressive "Squad." It is not social issues such as abortion or trans rights that are now in dispute; it is critical economic matters and comes as Democratic socialists make major strides in New York City and elsewhere. In New Mexico that dynamic is being manifested in several key proposals where the newly energized left parts ways with Haaland who is urging committee members to name Garcia Richard as her running mate rather than the more progressive Pope.--Private Equity Takeovers of PNM and the New Mexico Gas Company.Garcia RichardPope opposes Blackstone's proposed $11.5 billion acquisition of TXNM Energy, PNM’s parent  company. There is a similar private equity bid of $1.250 billion from Bernhard Capital Partners for the New Mexico Gas Company. Both takeovers await decisions from the Public Regulation Commission (PRC). Pope argues an unbridled thirst for profit by the bidders would ultimately "screw" ratepayers. He has joined protests outside PNM headquarters to condemn the  deals. Rather than just regulating the  private equity firms, Pope introduced Senate Memorial 9 urging  the PRC to pause the acquisitions. He also proposed a socialist alternative: having the state use its permanent funds to buy a majority stake in PNM and possibly a nonmajority stake in Gas Company. He argues this would keep utility profits in New Mexico and  diversify state revenue away from volatile oil and gas royalties. Haaland has focused her  platform on lower utility costs and holding public utilities accountable, rather than pushing for an outright state takeover of the  energy grid. While enviros have pressured the PRC to reject the Blackstone and BCP bids,  Haaland’s approach leans on enforcement of the state's  Energy Transition Act to ensure utility  profits don’t come at the expense of regular families, but she has  stopped short of endorsing Pope's state-ownership plan. Says Dem Central Committee member Mitchell Freedman of Rio Rancho:I continue to say this is an important political moment to show Deb  Haaland she and her consultants can't run the state like she ran the Democratic Party (as chairwoman) in 2016. The push for Pope is part of the Dem base revolt  against corporate Dem leadership and the consultants who simultaneously  fund and advise them.JUPITER On the massive Project Jupiter data center being built in Santa  Teresa, Pope, 52, wants the project halted, citing concerns about the  strain hyperscale data centers place on water resources and  the local energy grid. Jupiter will not tap into the local grid but  instead use natural gas fuel cells for power. But enviros assert the  center could still produce carbon  emissions equivalent to a coal-fired power plant. Pope is pushing for  regulatory interventions, including a statewide  data center moratorium as was recently done in New York state.In contrast Haaland supports a temporary pause on new data centers--but not Jupiter--while the state  drafts rules regarding water usage and grid demand. She says: "New Mexico is not a piggy bank and I  support our state putting guardrails in place that data centers must  follow...Large corporations must do their part. . .As governor, I’d  rather fix the guardrails than shut the door on an entire industry."Garcia Richard, 52, is actually more aligned with Pope than Haaland on Jupiter.. The Land Commissioner made recent headlines by halting a proposed natural gas line to  Jupiter that would run across state land--a direct blow to the project and more stern than Haaland's position. The bottom line on the divisions now on display in the Democratic party is whether the more insistent leftist positions on economic matters become more relevant in Santa Fe. Will there be state takeovers of gas and electric utilities previously thought inconceivable? A forever ban on data centers? A universal basic income for all residents which Pope has warmed to?Garcia Richard, with Haaland's blessing, has the edge over the more progressive Pope but no matter who wins the campaign has been revealing. The strain of socialist thinking we've seen in the nation in response to rampant income inequality and the increased cost of living is now a tangible, mainstream ideology in New Mexico. That's a first. How it plays out promises to be more suspenseful than the upcoming election. TRAIL DUSTFormer Las Cruces Mayor Ken Miyagishima has dropped his independent candidacy for governor after failing to collect 14,574 petition signatures needed to qualify for the November ballot, and he has thrown his support to Republican Gregg Hull. Miyagishima, a conservative Dem turned independent, toyed with filing a lawsuit to dispute the high number of signatures required of an independent candidate but decided not to. Still, that threshold, upheld in a long ago court ruling, could use anther going over in an era when registered independent voters now rival the number of registered Republicans. . .But hold on. There may be a court review yet. A federal lawsuit has been filed challenging the petition requirement that kept Bob Perls from running for the US Senate seat held by Sen. Ben Ray Lujan. Perls, chairman of the newly formed New Mexico Forward Party, filed suit over the requirement that he needed those 14,000 plus signatures to qualify for the ballot. He argues once the Forward Party submitted enough signatures to qualify as a minor party, they should have been allowed to place candidates on the ballot without a further petition requirement. The lawsuit and other info is here.Former ABQ city clerk and Dem state Sen. Katy Duhigg has a rebuttal: The statewide  signature requirement for independents and minor parties is much higher  than those for major party candidates because those independent and  minor party candidates get to skip running in a primary. It’s not a  plot, and it’s not unfair. It is the trade off for only having to run in  one election (the general election), instead of two (primary and  general). . . Dem US Rep. Gabe Vasquez holds a significant money lead over Republican Greg Cunningham in the race for the southern congressional seat. In the latest federal campaign reports Vasquez reports raising $569,000 and having nearly $2.4 million in cash on hand. Cunningham raised $382,000 and reported $768,000 in cash. The Cook Political report ranks the Second Congressional District lean Democrat. Polymarket bettors have Vasquez with an 85 percent chance of victory.This is the Home of New Mexico Politics.E-mail your news and comments. title: New Mexico AG Torrez seizes school discipline report to push woke reforms
body: New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez is using a new state report on school discipline in Gallup-McKinley County Schools to push a broader left-wing reform agenda, calling for changes to how schools punish students and urging lawmakers to give his office more power to investigate alleged civil rights violations. The report, released by the New Mexico Department of Justice, claims Gallup-McKinley schools have “substantial racial disparities” in suspensions and other discipline practices affecting Native American and Hispanic students. According to reporting from New Mexico In Depth and ProPublica, the investigation found that Indigenous students lose eight to 10 times more classroom days to suspension than white students, while Hispanic students lose three to four times as many. Gallup-McKinley County Schools is one of the largest geographically sprawling school districts in the state and serves part of the Navajo Nation. It also has the largest Native American student population of any public school district in the country. Torrez ordered the investigation in 2023 after earlier reporting by the same outlets claimed Native students in New Mexico were expelled at higher rates than other students. The reporting said Gallup-McKinley had about a quarter of New Mexico’s Native students but accounted for at least three-quarters of Native student expulsions during the four school years ending in 2020. Former Gallup-McKinley Superintendent Mike Hyatt previously dismissed those claims as “completely false,” arguing the findings were tied to data-entry errors and the district’s broad definition of expulsion. But Torrez’s investigators rejected that explanation, writing that neither the data issues nor the definition of expulsion accounted for the racial disparities found in the district. Now, the attorney general’s office is calling on the district to “acknowledge the facts” and work with the community on what the report described as “excessive reliance on exclusionary and discriminatory discipline.” The recommendations read like a wish list for progressive education reformers. The report urges Gallup-McKinley to more clearly define infractions, narrow discipline ranges, make punishments more “proportional,” limit suspensions, and adopt alternatives such as “restorative justice.” One example cited was “talking circles,” where students discuss how their behavior affected others, why they broke a rule, and what different choices they could have made. The Navajo Nation Human Rights Commission made similar recommendations in a March 2026 report accusing the district of discrimination. Commission Chair Wendy Greyeyes said neighboring districts already use some alternatives, though she acknowledged Gallup-McKinley may face challenges rebuilding trust with students and families. The attorney general’s report warned that unless the district changes course, “children in and around Gallup, along with their families and communities, will remain negatively affected by educational, social, and emotional challenges that stem from the District’s current practices.” Investigators also argued that suspensions do harm beyond academics, saying students removed from school can lose access to free meals, extracurriculars, clubs, and volunteer opportunities. The report pointed to national research linking suspensions and expulsions to lower academic achievement, greater contact with the criminal justice system, isolation, poor health, and lower wages. The findings come as schools across New Mexico continue struggling with classroom behavior, academic failure, truancy, and safety concerns. But instead of focusing primarily on restoring order and helping teachers maintain discipline, Torrez’s office is leaning into the increasingly common left-wing argument that discipline disparities are proof of systemic discrimination. The report also accused district leadership of denying problems and relying on flawed counter-analysis. “Instead of taking steps to rectify these problems, leadership denied that they exist and pushed a misleading and flawed counter-analysis,” the report said. Investigators further claimed the district provided a contract auditor with discipline data that was “inexplicably different” from what it had reported to state and federal education officials, with thousands of records allegedly missing. Gallup-McKinley Superintendent Jvanna Hanks II said the district is reviewing the report. “I am leading a period of transition that prioritizes community voices and renews our focus on every student,” Hanks wrote in a statement. “The School District will be using this report and current student data as part of our review. Our focus is that students should be in school, supported in school, and treated fairly in school.” But Torrez’s ambitions appear to go beyond one district. The report calls on state lawmakers and the New Mexico Public Education Department to strengthen statewide oversight of student discipline. It also recommends annual public audits of school discipline data. Anjana Samant, one of the report’s authors and a deputy director at the New Mexico Department of Justice, said such audits are needed to prevent disparities from becoming as “extreme and systemic as in Gallup-McKinley.” The report also urges lawmakers to revive legislation that would have given the attorney general’s office more authority to investigate and “identify and root out” civil rights violations. That bill passed in 2023, but Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham allowed it to die without her signature through a pocket veto. A spokesperson for the governor said she stands by that decision, citing concerns about whether the legislation “would have trumped federal student privacy protections and allowed the AG to access confidential student records.” For Torrez, the Gallup-McKinley report gives him a new platform to push for more power, more oversight, and more race-focused intervention in New Mexico schools. For parents and teachers, the question is whether these reforms will actually make classrooms safer and more functional — or simply make school discipline even harder in the name of woke ideology.
